title: Multi-Wavelength Signatures of a Giant Cometary Radio Halo in MACSJ0417-1154
comment: 24 pages (total), 24 figures, 6 tables, 3 appendix (6 figures). Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Galaxy clusters hosting diffuse non-thermal radio emission offer direct insight into plasma processes of the intracluster medium (ICM). We present the first multi-frequency study of the radio halo in MACSJ0417 (z = 0.445) using uGMRT (300-850 MHz), MeerKAT (900-1670 MHz), and archival \textit{XMM-Newton} data. The halo extends to $\sim$1.75 Mpc at 400 MHz, while two candidate relics (R1 and R2) are detected at 2.9 Mpc. The integrated spectra follow single power-laws with spectral indices $α\simeq -1.3$ for the halo and $α\simeq -1.6$ for the relics. Sensitive uGMRT imaging reveals a radio surface brightness edge $\sim$43$''$ SE of the cluster centre, which coincides with an X-ray discontinuity. Resolved spectral maps (400--1280 MHz) show significant fluctuations and a clear radial steepening of the spectral index. X-ray analysis reveals an elongated SE-NW morphology and high-temperature regions ($\sim$11 keV) along this axis. A strong radio and X-ray surface brightness correlation is found (correlation coefficient $\sim$ 0.85), with the correlation slope evolving from sublinear at 400 MHz to linear at 1280 MHz. These results, together with the spectral properties, support the turbulent re-acceleration model and point to inhomogeneous ICM conditions. The pure hadronic model is excluded owing to unrealistic energy requirements for cosmic-ray protons. We propose that MACSJ0417 is undergoing a minor off-axis dissociative merger (mass ratio $\sim$6:1) along the SE-NW axis, which has preserved its cool core while driving turbulence that powers the giant radio halo.

AI.tldr: Multi-frequency study of radio halo and relics in MACSJ0417 (z=0.445) using uGMRT, MeerKAT, and XMM-Newton. Halo extends ~1.75 Mpc, relics at 2.9 Mpc. Spectral indices α~-1.3 (halo) and α~-1.6 (relics). Strong radio-X-ray correlation (~0.85) supports turbulent re-acceleration; pure hadronic model excluded. Propose a minor off-axis dissociative merger (mass ratio ~6:1) powering the giant radio halo while preserving the cool core.
AI.motivation: To understand plasma processes in the intracluster medium (ICM) by studying diffuse non-thermal radio emission in galaxy clusters, providing the first multi-frequency analysis of the radio halo in MACSJ0417.
AI.method: Multi-frequency radio observations using uGMRT (300-850 MHz) and MeerKAT (900-1670 MHz) combined with archival XMM-Newton X-ray data. Performed spectral index mapping, surface brightness correlation analysis, and morphological comparisons between radio and X-ray emission.
AI.result: Halo extends to ~1.75 Mpc at 400 MHz; two candidate relics detected at 2.9 Mpc. Integrated spectra are single power-laws (α~-1.3 halo, α~-1.6 relics). A radio surface brightness edge coincides with an X-ray discontinuity. Spectral index shows radial steepening and fluctuations. Strong radio-X-ray correlation (~0.85) with slope evolving from sublinear to linear with frequency. High-temperature regions (~11 keV) along SE-NW axis.
AI.conclusion: Results support the turbulent re-acceleration model and exclude the pure hadronic model due to unrealistic cosmic-ray proton energy requirements. The cluster is undergoing a minor off-axis dissociative merger (mass ratio ~6:1) along SE-NW, preserving its cool core while driving turbulence that powers the giant radio halo.

title: Sub-Torque-Balance Upper Limits on Continuous Gravitational Waves from Scorpius X-1
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures
summary: We present the results of a search for continuous gravitational waves from the low-mass X-ray binary Scorpius X-1 using LIGO data from the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run. By applying the resampling version of the cross-correlation pipeline to search for signal frequencies $f_0$ between $25$ and $200\un{Hz}$ (corresponding to neutron star spin frequencies of $12.5$ to $100\un{Hz}$ for GW due to triaxiality, or $\sim15-20$ to $\sim120-150\un{Hz}$ for GW due to $r$-modes), we set upper limits below the standard torque balance level, independent of neutron star spin inclination, for $50\un{Hz}\lesssim f_0\lesssim200\un{Hz}$. While uncertainties in the modelling of torque and equation of state limit the strength of our inference, our results nonetheless argue against torque balance in this spin range for a neutron star described by a hadronic equation of state. The most sensitive upper limits on the gravitational wave amplitude $h_0$, at the upper end of the frequency band searched, approach $5\times10^{-26}$ marginalized over inclination angle and $2\times10^{-26}$ assuming the most favorable inclination. The marginalized upper limits correspond to a sensitivity depth of $70-75\un{Hz}^{-1/2}$, improving sensitivity considerably over previous searches. Expressed as constraints on the triaxial deformation of the neutron star, the limits correspond to an ellipticity of $3\times10^{-5}$ if the GW frequency $f_0$ is $75\un{Hz}$ and $3\times10^{-6}$ if $f_0=200\un{Hz}$, approaching deformations which could be supported by ordinary nuclear matter. Outliers from the search were ruled out as potential signals by a combination of hierarchical followup and analysis of additional data from later in the observing run.

AI.tldr: LIGO's fourth observing run searched for continuous gravitational waves from Scorpius X-1 using a cross-correlation pipeline, setting upper limits below the torque balance level for frequencies 50-200 Hz, with the most sensitive limit approaching h0 ~ 5×10⁻²⁶, ruling out torque balance for a hadronic equation of state neutron star in this spin range.
AI.motivation: To detect continuous gravitational waves from the low-mass X-ray binary Scorpius X-1, a promising source for such signals, using improved LIGO data from the fourth observing run.
AI.method: Applied the resampling version of the cross-correlation pipeline to LIGO data from O4's first part, searching for signal frequencies 25-200 Hz (covering both triaxial and r-mode GW emission), followed by hierarchical followup and analysis of additional data to rule out outliers.
AI.result: Set upper limits below the standard torque balance level (independent of spin inclination) for 50-200 Hz; most sensitive upper limits approach 5×10⁻²⁶ (marginalized over inclination) and 2×10⁻²⁶ (favorable inclination); sensitivity depth 70-75 Hz⁻¹/²; ellipticity constraints of 3×10⁻⁵ at 75 Hz and 3×10⁻⁶ at 200 Hz.
AI.conclusion: Results argue against torque balance in the 50-200 Hz spin range for a hadronic equation of state neutron star, though uncertainties in torque modeling and equation of state limit inference strength. Outliers were ruled out as potential signals.

title: The SANE, the MAD, and the Chimera
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures
summary: Non-radiative black hole accretion flows are commonly classified by their magnetic flux state, with standard and normal evolution (SANE) disks and magnetically arrested disks (MADs) marking the usual weak- and strong-flux regimes. We compare three-dimensional general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations of a weakly magnetized SANE flow, a standard MAD, and a Chimera flow fed by a different reservoir of mass, angular momentum, and coherent magnetic flux. The Chimera reaches a MAD-level horizon magnetic flux and launches a powerful electromagnetic jet during an extended non-eruptive interval, showing that a flow can maintain large horizon flux and jet power without sharing the standard MAD's bursty horizon-flux variability, mass-flow distribution, or inner-flow morphology. In the SANE flow, we show that radial support is primarily hydrodynamic and provided by gas pressure gradients, whereas in MAD flows, magnetic pressure and tension enter the radial force budget at comparable order and help regulate the inner flow dynamics. The Chimera remains distinct from the standard MAD in its density structure, funnel-wall geometry, mass-flow channels, radial force budget, and angular-momentum transport throughout the analyzed evolution. We therefore argue that MAD-like behavior is not captured by any single diagnostic, but by a dynamical coupling among horizon flux, jet power, magnetic support, Maxwell transport, surface-layer flow, disk morphology, and eruption activity. The Chimera shows that these outcomes can be separated by accretion history and magnetic-flux supply.

AI.tldr: Three 3D GRMHD simulations (SANE, MAD, Chimera) are compared. The Chimera achieves MAD-level horizon flux and jet power without the bursty variability and morphology of standard MADs, showing that accretion history and flux supply can decouple MAD-like diagnostics.
AI.motivation: To understand whether MAD-like behavior (strong magnetic flux, powerful jets) is uniquely associated with a specific dynamical state or can arise from different accretion histories and magnetic flux supplies.
AI.method: Comparison of three 3D general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations: a weakly magnetized SANE flow, a standard MAD, and a Chimera flow with a different reservoir of mass, angular momentum, and coherent magnetic flux.
AI.result: The Chimera reaches MAD-level horizon magnetic flux and launches a powerful electromagnetic jet without the bursty horizon-flux variability, mass-flow distribution, or inner-flow morphology typical of standard MADs. SANE radial support is primarily hydrodynamic (gas pressure gradients), while MAD flows involve magnetic pressure and tension at comparable order. The Chimera remains distinct in density structure, funnel-wall geometry, mass-flow channels, radial force budget, and angular-momentum transport.
AI.conclusion: MAD-like behavior is not captured by any single diagnostic but by a dynamical coupling of multiple outcomes (horizon flux, jet power, magnetic support, Maxwell transport, surface-layer flow, disk morphology, eruption activity). These outcomes can be separated by accretion history and magnetic-flux supply, as demonstrated by the Chimera.

title: Compact Objects Merging with Stars as an Origin of Ultra-Long Gamma-Ray Bursts and Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transients
comment: submitted to ApJL; comments welcome
summary: Ultra-long gamma-ray bursts (ULGRBs) and luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs) are two rare classes of engine-driven transients whose physical connection remains unknown. It has been suggested that both may arise from the mergers of a massive helium core with a compact object. We investigate this common origin by reanalyzing the optical counterpart of the highly unusual GRB 111209A/SN 2011kl associated with an ULGRB in the context of a recently developed, analytical LFBOT model. We find that SN 2011kl is broadly consistent with an LFBOT origin, exhibiting a rapid, luminous and blue early emission. However, compared to the LFBOT population, SN~2011kl features a longer "plateau" of emission ~2 weeks post-merger, suggesting an extended pre-merger mass-loss history, as well as stronger UV suppression. We additionally compare the host galaxy environments of five ULGRBs to those of LFBOTs and classical LGRBs. We find that ULGRBs, similar to LFBOTs and long GRBs, tend to occur in lower mass (<10^10 solar masses) galaxies with higher amounts of active star formation than observed for field galaxy populations at similar redshifts. Together, these results support a shared progenitor for at least a subset of ULGRBs and LFBOTs.

AI.tldr: This study investigates whether ultra-long gamma-ray bursts (ULGRBs) and luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs) share a common origin from mergers of massive helium cores with compact objects. By reanalyzing GRB 111209A/SN 2011kl, the authors find it broadly consistent with an LFBOT origin but with a longer plateau and stronger UV suppression. Host galaxy comparisons show ULGRBs, LFBOTs, and long GRBs all preferentially occur in low-mass, actively star-forming galaxies, supporting a shared progenitor for at least a subset of these transients.
AI.motivation: To determine the physical connection between ULGRBs and LFBOTs, two rare classes of engine-driven transients that may both arise from mergers of massive helium cores with compact objects.
AI.method: Reanalyzed the optical counterpart of GRB 111209A/SN 2011kl using an analytical LFBOT model, and compared host galaxy environments of five ULGRBs to those of LFBOTs and classical long GRBs.
AI.result: SN 2011kl is broadly consistent with an LFBOT origin (rapid, luminous, blue early emission) but shows a longer ~2-week plateau and stronger UV suppression. ULGRB host galaxies are similar to LFBOT and long GRB hosts: low-mass (<10^10 Msun), actively star-forming galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The results support a shared progenitor for at least a subset of ULGRBs and LFBOTs.

title: Supersonic Motion in the Driving Region of M82
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The prototypical starburst galaxy M82 is host to an expansive, multiphase outflow whose driving mechanism is not fully understood. Longstanding models suggest that energy and mass injection from supernova into the hottest phase of the galactic wind could drive the cooler phases, but validating these models has been difficult due to the lack of constraints on the hot wind energetics. The high-resolution spectral capabilities of XRISM have generated the tightest constraints to date on the temperatures of the hot wind, as well as the first direct measurement of its velocity dispersion. In this work, we use these new observational constraints to test a model of a supernova-driven free wind. We generate a suite of highly idealized hydrodynamic simulations varying the energy and mass loading of the starburst and construct mock spectra to compare against the XRISM results. We find that the observed velocity dispersion is impossible to replicate using our free-wind model alone, and extra broadening is required to fit the spectrum. We interpret this broadening to be due not to bulk outflow, but rather to smaller scale non-thermal motions in the driving region of the starburst. This implies supersonic motion (Mach 1.71-3.14) of the hot gas in the central region of the galaxy. As supersonic motions are unexpected, it is possible that a significant amount of the energy that should go into heating the gas is instead going towards other sources such as amplifying magnetic fields and driving cosmic rays.

AI.tldr: Using XRISM observations of M82's hot wind, the authors find that a supernova-driven free-wind model cannot replicate the observed velocity dispersion, requiring additional broadening from non-thermal motions (Mach 1.71-3.14) in the starburst core, suggesting energy is diverted to magnetic fields and cosmic rays rather than heating the gas.
AI.motivation: To understand the driving mechanism of M82's multiphase outflow by testing supernova-driven wind models against new XRISM constraints on hot wind temperature and velocity dispersion.
AI.method: The authors generate idealized hydrodynamic simulations with varying energy and mass loading, construct mock X-ray spectra, and compare them directly to XRISM observations of M82's hot wind.
AI.result: The free-wind model cannot reproduce the observed velocity dispersion; extra broadening from non-thermal motions (Mach 1.71-3.14) is required, implying supersonic hot gas motions in the galactic center.
AI.conclusion: Supersonic non-thermal motions in the starburst core indicate that supernova energy is partially diverted from gas heating to other processes (magnetic field amplification, cosmic ray acceleration), challenging standard wind-driving models.

title: Multi-wavelength Constraints on the Transient EP250905a
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are a diverse class of high-energy suggested origins, ranging from stellar explosions to compact object mergers. The Einstein Probe (EP) satellite discovers approximately 100 FXTs per year. We aim to constrain the physical origin of EP250905a. We analyze X-ray, optical, near-infrared (NIR), and radio temporal and spectral properties of EP250905a. In addition, we assess the possible role of weak gravitational lensing in shaping its observed characteristics. EP250905a fades rapidly in X-rays, and we detect no NIR or radio emission, but we detect early optical emission that rapidly fades beyond the detection limits. Two nearby galaxies are identified for which we derive spectroscopic redshifts of $z=0.374$ (G1) and $z=2.714$ (G2). Our analysis favors G2 as the host of the FXT EP250905a. The angular separation of 2.56\arcsec\, between the FXT's optical counterpart and the center of the G1 galaxy suggests the emission of the FXT might be moderately magnified by lensing effects ($μ\approx3.9$) given the inferred Einstein radius of G1 ($θ_E\approx1.9$ arcsec). The data are best explained as an afterglow from a mildly off-axis structured jet at $z=2.714$, providing a consistent broadband interpretation that also allows for weakly lensed emission of EP250905a.

AI.tldr: EP250905a is a fast X-ray transient discovered by Einstein Probe, likely a mildly off-axis structured jet afterglow at z=2.714, with possible weak gravitational lensing (μ≈3.9) by a foreground galaxy at z=0.374.
AI.motivation: To constrain the physical origin of the fast X-ray transient EP250905a, given the diverse possible origins of FXTs and the large number (~100/yr) being discovered by the Einstein Probe.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength (X-ray, optical, NIR, radio) temporal and spectral analysis; spectroscopic redshift measurements of two nearby galaxies; gravitational lensing analysis using the Einstein radius of the foreground galaxy.
AI.result: EP250905a shows rapid X-ray fading, early optical emission that fades below detection limits, and no detected NIR or radio emission. Two galaxies at z=0.374 (G1) and z=2.714 (G2) are identified; G2 is favored as the host. Potential weak lensing by G1 (μ≈3.9, θ_E≈1.9 arcsec, separation 2.56 arcsec).
AI.conclusion: The broadband data are best explained as a mildly off-axis structured jet afterglow at z=2.714, with possible weak lensing magnification, providing a consistent physical interpretation for EP250905a.

title: Probing the origins. III. Exoplanet demographics across Galactic birth radii
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome. Abridged abstract to fit ArXiv's requirements
summary: We quantify radial mixing in exoplanet hosts and explore links between birth environment, orbital evolution, planetary architecture, and Galactic habitability. We constructed a homogeneous catalogue by cross-matching the Encyclopaedia of Exoplanetary Systems with Gaia DR3 astrometry and infrared photometry from 2MASS and AllWISE. Stellar orbits were integrated using Galpy. Stellar birth radii were inferred by combining Galactic chemical enrichment models with the generalised additive model introduced in Paper I. Giant-planet hosts preferentially trace inner-Galaxy birth sites, whereas brown-dwarf hosts span a broader, less localised range of radial displacements. Rocky-only systems show smaller radial excursions and less centrally concentrated birth radii, while rocky+giant systems are intermediate, retaining a stronger link to inner-disc birth environments than rocky-only systems. We also find that outward-migrators host more compact outer detected companions than inward-migrators, with non-migrators in between. This trend remains tentative because of heterogeneous detection biases. Giant-planet hosts retain a strong connection to metal-rich inner-Galaxy birth environments, whereas brown-dwarf hosts span a broader range of radial displacements, and rocky-only systems are less centrally concentrated. The older ages of rocky and rocky+giant hosts, especially among outward migrators, make them useful reference populations for future habitability and technosignature searches. Dynamically heated outer-Galaxy-born hosts show that planet-hosting systems can survive significant Galactic perturbations, although whether their architectures retain causal imprints of this evolution remains uncertain. No clear connection is found between radial displacement and the number of detected planets.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies radial mixing in exoplanet hosts by cross-matching exoplanet catalogs with Gaia DR3 data, finding that giant-planet hosts originate from inner-Galaxy birth sites, brown-dwarf hosts show broader radial displacements, and rocky-only systems have smaller excursions. Outward-migrators host more compact outer companions, and older rocky/rocky+giant hosts are useful for future habitability searches.
AI.motivation: To understand how radial mixing and birth environments of stars influence exoplanet architectures, orbital evolution, and Galactic habitability.
AI.method: Cross-matched Encyclopaedia of Exoplanetary Systems with Gaia DR3 astrometry, 2MASS, and AllWISE photometry; used Galpy for stellar orbit integration; inferred birth radii via Galactic chemical enrichment models combined with a generalized additive model from a prior study.
AI.result: Giant-planet hosts preferentially trace inner-Galaxy birth sites; brown-dwarf hosts span broader radial displacements; rocky-only systems show smaller radial excursions; outward-migrators host more compact outer companions; older ages found for rocky and rocky+giant hosts, especially outward migrators.
AI.conclusion: Giant-planet hosts retain strong connection to metal-rich inner-Galaxy birth environments; dynamically heated outer-Galaxy-born hosts survive significant Galactic perturbations; no clear connection between radial displacement and detected planet multiplicity; rocky/rocky+giant hosts (particularly outward migrators) are useful for future habitability and technosignature searches.

title: The Southern-sky MWA Rapid Two-metre (SMART) pulsar survey--IV. Survey update and an atlas of 205 non-recycled southern pulsars
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables; Accepted for publication in PASA
summary: The SMART survey is an ambitious effort to conduct sensitive searches for pulsars and fast transients at 140-170 MHz. The novelty of voltage recording, long dwell times and the high-time and -frequency resolutions exchange a large survey speed for high computational cost. The survey covers the entire sky south of +30 degree in declination through a series of dedicated campaigns, accumulating 4 PB of data. The large volumes of data necessitate processing to be approached in multiple phases, and the initial searches focused on a shallow survey of parts of the skies, as reported in earlier papers. These data are also processed for re-detections of hundreds of known pulsars in the southern sky, many of which are also the first detections below 400 MHz. This paper is motivated by the need to address the inherent difficulties in handling large amounts of voltage data and software/processing challenges for routine pulsar detections, and also by the fast-evolving landscape of the SKA Observatory (SKAO). With the construction ramping up towards the full-scale SKA-Low, a low-frequency catalogue of detectable pulsars in the southern sky will prove to be a valuable reference for science verification. A growing sample of low-frequency detections and measurements will also prove invaluable in a variety of science applications including population studies, survey simulations and emission beam models, refining interstellar medium models for electron densities and the spatial distribution of turbulence, and also for forecasting the detection prospects and survey yield from pulsar surveys planned with SKA-Low. We present various data products, including pulse profiles, time series and multi-channel folded archives, along with the measurements of dispersion and rotation measures, and mean flux densities, and this will be periodically updated as more detections flow on from the ongoing data processing.

AI.tldr: The SMART survey processes 4 PB of voltage data at 140-170 MHz to detect pulsars and fast transients across the southern sky. This paper presents data products (pulse profiles, time series, multi-channel folded archives) and measurements (DM, RM, mean flux densities) from hundreds of known pulsar redetections—many first detections below 400 MHz—motivated by the need to handle large voltage data processing challenges and to provide a low-frequency reference catalogue for SKA-Low science verification.
AI.motivation: Address inherent difficulties in handling large amounts of voltage data and software/processing challenges for routine pulsar detections; support the fast-evolving SKA Observatory (SKAO) by providing a low-frequency catalogue of detectable southern-sky pulsars as a reference for SKA-Low science verification, population studies, survey simulations, emission beam models, and interstellar medium modelling.
AI.method: Voltage recording with long dwell times and high time/frequency resolution; multi-phase processing of 4 PB of data; dedicated campaigns covering the entire sky south of +30° declination; initial shallow surveys followed by re-detection of hundreds of known pulsars; production of pulse profiles, time series, multi-channel folded archives, and measurements of dispersion measures (DM), rotation measures (RM), and mean flux densities.
AI.result: Hundreds of known pulsars redetected in the southern sky, many first detections below 400 MHz; growing sample of low-frequency detections and measurements; data products include pulse profiles, time series, multi-channel folded archives, DM, RM, and mean flux densities; catalogue will be periodically updated.
AI.conclusion: The SMART survey provides a valuable low-frequency reference catalogue of detectable pulsars in the southern sky for SKA-Low science verification, population studies, survey simulations, emission beam models, and interstellar medium modelling. The data products and measurements will be updated as more detections are processed.

title: Tracing black hole and galaxy growth across environments since cosmic noon
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures. Under review at ApJ
summary: The distribution of systems in the black hole mass-stellar mass ($M_\mathrm{BH}-M_\star$) plane encodes not only the integrated growth of galaxies and their central black holes (BHs), but also the processes that shape their evolution. Using the ASTRID and TNG300 cosmological simulations, we track massive BHs from cosmic noon ($z=2$) to $z=0.5$, spanning 5.3 Gyr of assembly. Unlike most previous studies, we follow the BHs themselves rather than their original host galaxies, thereby capturing central BHs, BHs in satellites, and off-nuclear wandering BHs. We find that central BHs in both simulations evolve along a relatively tight, nearly redshift-invariant $M_\mathrm{BH}-M_\star$ relation that is broadly consistent with local empirical constraints and with measurements from variable active galactic nuclei (AGN) at comparable redshifts. Departures from this relation trace distinct evolutionary channels. High-mass central BHs grow substantially through mergers and subsequently quench their hosts through AGN kinetic feedback. Tidal stripping moves satellites to lower $M_\star$ at nearly fixed $M_\mathrm{BH}$, producing weakly accreting, overmassive central BHs in gas-poor systems. In ASTRID, satellite accretion and inefficient dynamical friction generate wandering BHs that are undermassive relative to their new hosts and experience minimal accretion or merger-driven growth. These populations occupy characteristic regions in both the $M_\mathrm{BH}-M_\star$ and the specific BH accretion rate-specific star formation rate planes, demonstrating that a BH's location in these planes is a fossil record of its dynamical, accretion, and feedback history.

AI.tldr: Using ASTRID and TNG300 simulations, this paper tracks massive black holes from z=2 to z=0.5 and shows that the M_BH-M_star plane encodes the dynamical, accretion, and feedback history of BHs—including central, satellite, and wandering populations—with distinct evolutionary channels (mergers, tidal stripping, satellite accretion) producing characteristic offsets from the redshift-invariant main relation.
AI.motivation: To understand how the distribution of systems in the M_BH-M_star plane encodes integrated BH-galaxy growth and the processes shaping their evolution, by following BHs themselves (not just their hosts) across cosmic time.
AI.method: Analyzed massive BHs from z=2 to z=0.5 (5.3 Gyr) in the ASTRID and TNG300 cosmological simulations, tracking central BHs, BHs in satellites, and off-nuclear wandering BHs individually across time.
AI.result: Central BHs follow a tight, nearly redshift-invariant M_BH-M_star relation consistent with local constraints and AGN variability measurements. High-mass central BHs grow via mergers and quench hosts via AGN kinetic feedback. Tidal stripping produces overmassive central BHs in gas-poor satellites. Wandering BHs in ASTRID are undermassive with minimal accretion/merger growth.
AI.conclusion: A BH's location in the M_BH-M_star and sBHAR-sSFR planes serves as a fossil record of its dynamical, accretion, and feedback history, with characteristic regions traced by distinct evolutionary channels.

title: A Magnetar Engine and Circumstellar Medium Interaction: Synergistic Effects in Producing Superluminous Supernovae
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Superluminous supernovae (SLSNe) are often modeled as being powered either by a central engine or by strong interaction with dense circumstellar material (CSM). These two mechanisms may be dynamically coupled if the ejecta interact with dense CSM while being energized by a newborn magnetar. We develop a semi-analytical hybrid model that follows the coupled dynamics, energy conversion, and radiative output of such systems. A rapidly rotating magnetar injects energy through a relativistic wind, inflating a hot bubble inside the expanding ejecta. Part of the injected energy is stored as radiation, while the rest is converted into bulk kinetic energy of the swept-up ejecta. At the same time, the outer ejecta collide with the surrounding CSM and form a circumstellar interaction (CSI) region. As the shock driven by the magnetar accelerates through the ejecta, it can catch up with the CSI region and take over the subsequent interaction with the unshocked CSM. The emergent light curves are therefore governed by the coupled effects of magnetar energy injection, shock heating, and radiative diffusion. We show that this hybrid model can produce diverse SLSN light-curve morphologies, including luminous interaction-powered peaks, asymmetric post-peak declines, and late-time emission sustained by delayed leakage of magnetar-powered radiation. The model provides a plausible way to reduce the extreme nickel-mass or initial explosion-energy requirements often encountered in purely radioactive or purely interaction-powered interpretations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a semi-analytical hybrid model for superluminous supernovae that combines magnetar central engine powering with circumstellar interaction, showing this coupled mechanism can produce diverse light-curve morphologies and reduce extreme energy/nickel requirements of single-mechanism models.
AI.motivation: SLSNe are typically modeled as powered either by a central engine (magnetar) or by strong CSM interaction, but these mechanisms may be dynamically coupled when ejecta interact with dense CSM while being energized by a newborn magnetar. Existing single-mechanism models often require extreme nickel masses or explosion energies.
AI.method: A semi-analytical hybrid model that tracks coupled dynamics, energy conversion, and radiative output. It includes: (1) magnetar injection via relativistic wind inflating a hot bubble inside ejecta, (2) outer ejecta-CSM collision forming a CSI region, and (3) the magnetar-driven shock potentially catching up with and taking over the CSI interaction.
AI.result: The hybrid model produces diverse SLSN light-curve morphologies: luminous interaction-powered peaks, asymmetric post-peak declines, and late-time emission from delayed magnetar-powered radiation leakage. It reduces the extreme nickel-mass or initial explosion-energy requirements of purely radioactive or purely interaction-powered models.
AI.conclusion: The coupled magnetar+CSI hybrid model offers a more physically realistic and economical explanation for SLSNe, reducing reliance on extreme parameters required by single-mechanism interpretations.

title: The incidence of eROSITA X-ray AGN in the local Universe: from dwarf to massive galaxies
comment: 27 pages, 20 figures; accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Combining deep, wide-area X-ray surveys with multi-wavelength catalogues provides insights into rare, highly-accreting AGN and low-mass galaxies at low redshift, the latter potentially representing local analogues of the first galaxies in the early Universe. We use the four-pass eROSITA All Sky Survey to select the largest catalogue of X-ray AGN in a highly complete sample of low-redshift galaxies, including low-mass (logM*/Msol<10) ones. We probe their distribution of specific accretion rates, $λ$_SAR, and the cumulative AGN fraction above varying $λ$_SAR thresholds. Our parent sample consists of ~5.35 million galaxies selected from the Legacy Survey DR10 with z-band fluxes brighter than 20 mag and redshifts 0.03<z<0.2. We place particular emphasis on the detailed characterisation of our sample, including estimating unbiased physical galaxy properties and rigorous cleaning and validation of the X-ray aperture photometry and host-galaxy associations. We identify 874 X-ray AGN in low-mass galaxies, most of them newly discovered as X-ray emitters. Thanks to a Bayesian framework that makes use of the X-ray information from all parent sample galaxies, we constrain the specific accretion rate distribution, p(log$λ$_SAR | M*, z), across a wide range of $λ$_SAR and uncover second-order mass-dependent effects. We detect a break at high $λ$_SAR, possibly indicating Eddington-limited, self-regulated black hole growth. Integrating p(log$λ$_SAR | M*, z) above $λ$_SAR>10^-3, we find a cumulative AGN fraction of ~1% for low-mass galaxies, placing a firm lower limit on the black hole occupation fraction in this regime. Overall, our specific accretion rate distributions, sampling down to the as-of-yet unexplored low-mass regime, highlight a more nuanced, mass-dependent view of AGN growth and accretion history that must be taken into account in future modelling.

AI.tldr: This paper uses eROSITA X-ray data and Legacy Survey optical data to construct the largest catalogue of X-ray AGN in low-redshift galaxies, including ~874 low-mass galaxies. Using Bayesian modeling, the authors constrain the specific accretion rate distribution down to the low-mass regime (logM*/Msol<10), find a break at high λ_SAR indicative of Eddington-limited growth, and report a cumulative AGN fraction of ~1% for low-mass galaxies above λ_SAR>10^-3, placing a firm lower limit on black hole occupation fraction.
AI.motivation: To probe the distribution of specific accretion rates and AGN fraction in low-redshift galaxies, particularly low-mass galaxies (logM*/Msol<10), which may serve as local analogues of the first galaxies in the early Universe. The study aims to uncover mass-dependent effects in AGN growth and accretion history that have been unexplored in the low-mass regime.
AI.method: Cross-matching four-pass eROSITA All Sky Survey X-ray data with ~5.35 million galaxies from Legacy Survey DR10 (z-band <20 mag, 0.03<z<0.2). Rigorous cleaning and validation of X-ray aperture photometry and host-galaxy associations. A Bayesian framework constrains the specific accretion rate distribution p(logλ_SAR | M*, z) across a wide range, using X-ray information from all parent sample galaxies.
AI.result: Identified 874 X-ray AGN in low-mass galaxies (most newly discovered). Detected a break at high λ_SAR, possibly indicating Eddington-limited, self-regulated black hole growth. Found a cumulative AGN fraction of ~1% for low-mass galaxies above λ_SAR>10^-3, placing a firm lower limit on the black hole occupation fraction in this regime.
AI.conclusion: The specific accretion rate distributions highlight a nuanced, mass-dependent view of AGN growth and accretion history that must be incorporated into future modeling. The low-mass regime has been explored down to previously unexplored levels.

title: Exploring the effect of mixing in Low-Luminosity Type IIp Supernovae by modeling SN 2024abfl
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Low-luminosity Type IIp supernovae (LLSNe) are SN IIps with peak magnitudes > -15.5 and plateau magnitudes between -13.5 and -15.5 in the V band. SN 2024abfl is an LLSN with a unique light curve, particularly the steep drop in luminosity observed after the plateau phase makes it an interesting candidate for modeling core-collapse supernova mechanisms. Using a custom pipeline involving MESA and STELLA, we investigate the possibility of suppressed ejecta mixing as a cause of the steep drop-off from the plateau phase. We find that turning off mixing mechanisms during shock breakout can mimic the distinct flat plateau and steep luminosity drop into the radioactive tail of the light curve while using previously proposed progenitor mass, radius and explosion energy parameters. Using these results as a proof-of-concept, exploring the effects of limited mixing in LLSNe candidates could give us better insight into how they differ from Typical Type IIp SNe.

AI.tldr: SN 2024abfl, a low-luminosity Type IIp supernova, exhibits a distinct steep drop after the plateau phase. Using MESA and STELLA simulations, the authors find that suppressed mixing during shock breakout can reproduce this light curve feature, offering a proof-of-concept that limited mixing may distinguish LLSNe from typical Type IIp SNe.
AI.motivation: To understand the unique steep luminosity drop in the light curve of SN 2024abfl, an LLSN candidate, and investigate whether suppressed ejecta mixing can explain this distinct post-plateau behavior.
AI.method: Custom pipeline using MESA (stellar evolution) and STELLA (radiation hydrodynamics) to model core-collapse supernova light curves; mixing mechanisms are turned off during shock breakout to test their effect on the plateau-to-radioactive tail transition.
AI.result: Suppressing mixing mechanisms during shock breakout successfully replicates the flat plateau and steep luminosity drop into the radioactive tail, consistent with previously proposed progenitor parameters (mass, radius, explosion energy).
AI.conclusion: Limited ejecta mixing may be a key mechanism distinguishing LLSNe from typical Type IIp SNe; this proof-of-concept motivates further exploration of mixing effects in low-luminosity supernova candidates.

title: Boötes III is a Tidally Disrupting Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxy on an Eccentric Polar Orbit
comment: 32 pages, 15 figures, 7 tables. To be submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics. Analysis code and data available at https://github.com/s5collab/boo3
summary: We present updated systemic properties of the ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes III from the Southern Stellar Stream Spectroscopic Survey (S$^5$). We identify 21 high-probability members and measure a velocity dispersion of $σ_{v} = 1.69^{+1.03}_{-0.85}$ km s$^{-1}$, about six times smaller than the previously reported $10.7 \pm 3.5$ km s$^{-1}$, and a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] $= -2.34 \pm 0.11$. The revised dispersion brings Boötes III in line with other tidally disrupting dwarfs such as Antlia II and Crater II. Orbit integrations in a Milky Way (MW) + Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) potential confirm a highly eccentric ($e \approx 0.8$), polar ($i \approx 89.5^\circ$) orbit with a recent pericentric passage $\sim 0.14$ Gyr ago at $r_{\rm peri} \approx 9.5$ kpc. Boötes III is thus likely actively tidally disrupting, as its tidal radius at pericenter, $r_t \approx 164$ pc, is only $\sim 0.35$ of its half-light radius. The unusually low dispersion also implies that Boötes III has either lost most of its dark matter to tides or hosts a cored inner density profile, making it a probe of the nature of dark matter. Simulated tidal streams are broadly consistent with the Styx stellar stream, though the predicted track and kinematics are sensitive to the MW halo mass, LMC mass, and solar velocity. Boötes III overlaps the Typhon stream in integrals-of-motion space but has a much lower mean metallicity, suggesting the two are not the same system but may have had a common group infall origin. Sagittarius-stream contamination prevents a direct tidal-tail detection, so deep spectroscopic follow-up remains essential, both to confirm Styx as a genuine stream and to establish it as Boötes III's tidal tail.

AI.tldr: The ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes III has a much smaller velocity dispersion (1.69 km/s) than previously reported (10.7 km/s), making it consistent with other tidally disrupting dwarfs. It follows a highly eccentric polar orbit and is likely actively losing its dark matter to tides, testing cored vs. cuspy dark matter profiles. Its tidal streams may be linked to the Styx stream, while the Typhon stream is chemically distinct but possibly co-infalling.
AI.motivation: To refine the systemic properties of the ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes III using high-quality spectroscopic data from S$^5$, given that previous measurements gave anomalously high velocity dispersion, and to assess its tidal disruption status and dark matter content.
AI.method: Identification of 21 high-probability members from S$^5$ spectroscopy; measurement of velocity dispersion and mean metallicity; orbit integration in a MW + LMC potential; comparison of tidal radius to half-light radius; simulation of tidal streams.
AI.result: Velocity dispersion = 1.69^{+1.03}_{-0.85} km/s (six times smaller than previous 10.7 km/s); mean [Fe/H] = -2.34 ± 0.11; highly eccentric (e~0.8), polar orbit with recent pericenter ~0.14 Gyr ago at ~9.5 kpc; tidal radius at pericenter (164 pc) is ~0.35 of half-light radius; Boötes III likely tidally disrupting and dark-matter-depleted or cored.
AI.conclusion: Boötes III is a tidally disrupting ultra-faint dwarf with a low velocity dispersion, consistent with other disrupting dwarfs. Its properties make it a probe of dark matter (cored vs. cuspy). The Styx stream is a plausible tidal tail but sensitive to MW/LMC mass assumptions. Typhon stream is chemically distinct but may share infall origin. Deep spectroscopy is needed to confirm the stream association.

title: The 20 GeV Galactic Halo Excess: Pixel-Level Confirmation and Consistency with Sub-TeV WIMP Annihilation
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures
summary: A recent analysis of 15 years of Fermi-LAT data reported a spherically symmetric, halo-like component of the Galactic diffuse emission that peaks near 20GeV. We independently reproduce this cell-aggregated analysis, then extend it to a pixel-level likelihood on the native $0.125^\circ$ maps, adding energy-dependent point-spread-function forward folding and masking bright sources. Both methods replicate the 20GeV halo spectrum, with the pixel-level normalisation ${\sim}20\%$ above the cellwise fit across NFW emissivity scalings $ρ^p$, $p \in 1,2,2.5$. This 20GeV halo is a high-latitude feature, distinct from the inner-Galaxy excess, and consistent with sub-TeV dark matter (WIMP) annihilation. It is centrally concentrated, strongly disfavouring extragalactic emission. Fitting prompt $s$-wave annihilation spectra, best-fit masses are $m_χ\simeq 0.55$TeV ($W^+W^-$) and $0.72$TeV ($b\bar{b}$) with $\langleσv\rangle \simeq 1\times10^{-24}~\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$, in $\sim\!4$-$5\times$ tension with dwarf spheroidal galaxy limits. However, accounting for foreground modelling and $J$-factor systematic uncertainties widens the tension window to $R\simeq1.6$-$9.3$, leaving the $s$-wave interpretation viable. To close the tension, we consider alternative particle dark matter models. $p$-wave annihilation misses relic abundance constraints by $\sim\!7$ orders of magnitude. A decay interpretation evades dwarf limits but is disfavoured by the isotropic gamma-ray background. The only viable velocity structure consistent with dwarf limits, present-day halo rates, and relic density is low-velocity-enhanced annihilation (resonant Sommerfeld or Breit-Wigner). This supplies the required $\approx\!45\times$ boost from a thermal relic. Fully resolving the dwarf tension requires a fine-tuned resonance peaking at the halo velocity and falling for colder systems.

AI.tldr: A reanalysis of 15 years of Fermi-LAT data confirms a spherically symmetric 20 GeV gamma-ray halo consistent with sub-TeV dark matter annihilation. Best-fit s-wave WIMP models (mχ≈0.55-0.72 TeV, ⟨σv⟩~10^{-24} cm³/s) show 4-5× tension with dwarf spheroidal limits, but accounting for systematics widens the tension window (R≈1.6-9.3), leaving s-wave viable. Alternative models: p-wave fails relic abundance by ~7 orders; decay is disfavored by isotropic gamma-ray background. Only low-velocity-enhanced annihilation (resonant Sommerfeld/Breit-Wigner) can reconcile dwarf limits, halo rates, and relic density, requiring a ≈45× boost from thermal relic and fine-tuning at halo velocities.
AI.motivation: To independently reproduce and extend a recent analysis of Fermi-LAT data that reported a 20 GeV spherically symmetric halo-like component of Galactic diffuse emission, and to assess its viability as a dark matter signal given constraints from dwarf spheroidal galaxies, relic abundance, and the isotropic gamma-ray background.
AI.method: Reproduced cell-aggregated analysis of 15 years of Fermi-LAT data, then extended to pixel-level likelihood on native 0.125° maps with energy-dependent PSF forward folding and bright source masking. Compared cellwise vs. pixel-level fits across NFW emissivity scalings ρ^p (p∈1,2,2.5). Fitted prompt s-wave annihilation spectra and tested alternative DM models: p-wave annihilation, decay, and velocity-enhanced annihilation (resonant Sommerfeld/Breit-Wigner).
AI.result: Both methods replicate the 20 GeV halo spectrum (pixel-level normalization ~20% above cellwise). The halo is a high-latitude feature distinct from the inner-Galaxy excess, centrally concentrated (disfavoring extragalactic origin). Best-fit s-wave WIMP: mχ≈0.55 TeV (W+W-) and 0.72 TeV (bb̄) with ⟨σv⟩≈1×10^{-24} cm³/s, in ~4-5× tension with dwarf limits (tension window R≈1.6-9.3 with systematics). p-wave misses relic abundance by ~7 orders. Decay disfavored by isotropic gamma-ray background. Only low-velocity-enhanced annihilation (resonant Sommerfeld/Breit-Wigner) reconciles all constraints, requiring ~45× boost from thermal relic and fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The 20 GeV halo is robustly confirmed as a high-latitude, centrally concentrated feature consistent with sub-TeV dark matter annihilation. While s-wave models face moderate tension with dwarf limits, accounting for systematics keeps them viable. The most promising interpretation is low-velocity-enhanced annihilation (resonant Sommerfeld or Breit-Wigner), which can satisfy dwarf limits, present-day halo rates, and relic density simultaneously, albeit with fine-tuning at halo velocities.

title: Scaling Relations for Binary Black Hole Merger Times from Cosmological Initial Conditions
comment: 21 pages, 16 figures
summary: Recent evidence from Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) for a nanohertz gravitational wave background is broadly consistent with theoretical expectations from a population of massive black hole binaries (MBHBs), although the inferred amplitude appears somewhat higher than predicted by standard models. Interpreting these observations requires a robust understanding of the merger timescales of MBHBs, and of their connection to host galaxy properties. In this work, we investigate the evolution of MBHBs selected from cosmological galaxy mergers in the IllustrisTNG simulation. We re-simulate these systems at high resolution using the N-body code Griffin to accurately resolve the dynamical friction and stellar hardening phases, and follow their evolution to coalescence with a semi-analytical model. We find that cosmological galaxy encounters and the resulting MBHBs are typically highly eccentric. We characterise the distribution of binary eccentricities at formation and at entry into the PTA band, and quantify the corresponding residence times. We identify the key parameters governing the duration of the different stages of MBHB evolution, and derive scaling relations linking galaxy and orbital properties to dynamical friction, hardening, and total coalescence times. These relations provide a framework for subgrid prescriptions in cosmological simulations. Applying these scaling relations to the full IllustrisTNG merger population, we infer the probability distributions of galaxy merger and black hole coalescence times. We find that galaxy mergers typically complete within $\sim 0.7$ Gyr, while the total black hole coalescence time is $\sim 1.0$ Gyr. These short timescales imply efficient binary evolution, consistent with current PTA constraints.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution N-body simulations of MBHBs from IllustrisTNG, this study finds highly eccentric binaries, short coalescence times (~1.0 Gyr for black holes, ~0.7 Gyr for galaxies), and derives scaling relations linking galaxy properties to binary evolution stages, consistent with PTA observations of a nanohertz gravitational wave background.
AI.motivation: PTA observations suggest a gravitational wave background amplitude higher than standard model predictions, necessitating a robust understanding of MBHB merger timescales and their connection to host galaxy properties to correctly interpret these signals.
AI.method: MBHBs are selected from cosmological galaxy mergers in IllustrisTNG, re-simulated at high resolution with the N-body code Griffin to resolve dynamical friction and stellar hardening, then evolved to coalescence via a semi-analytical model.
AI.result: Cosmological MBHBs are typically highly eccentric; galaxy mergers complete within ~0.7 Gyr and total black hole coalescence within ~1.0 Gyr. Scaling relations linking galaxy/orbital properties to coalescence times are derived.
AI.conclusion: Short merger timescales imply efficient binary evolution consistent with current PTA constraints, and the derived scaling relations provide a framework for subgrid prescriptions in cosmological simulations.

title: FAST Discovery of $μ$Jy Radio Pulsations from PSR J2238+5903, Providing a DM Distance Anchor for the Candidate TeV Halo 1LHAASO J2238+5900
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, comments welcome
summary: We report the first detection of radio pulsations from PSR J2238+5903, a gamma-ray pulsar spatially coincident with the extended TeV source 1LHAASO J2238+5900. Our 3000 s FAST L-band observation reveals a weak periodic signal at the known Fermi-LAT spin period, with $P=162.76568$ ms and $\mathrm{DM}=247.5\pm3.0~\mathrm{pc~cm^{-3}}$. The signal is independently confirmed by both FFT-based and Fast Folding Algorithm searches. The radiometer equation gives a flux density of $S_{1250}\simeq3\,μ$Jy, placing PSR J2238+5903 among the faintest radio-detected Fermi pulsars. Interpreting the DM with Galactic electron-density models gives $d_{\rm DM}=7.4\pm3.9$ kpc. At this distance, the LHAASO WCDA 39\% containment radius corresponds to a characteristic diameter of $\sim132$ pc, and the $>1$ TeV luminosity is $L_{\rm TeV}\simeq7.1\times10^{34}$ erg s$^{-1}$, about 8\% of the pulsar's spin-down power. The radio DM thus provides the first pulsar-specific distance constraint for assessing whether 1LHAASO J2238+5900 is a young relic-PWN / TeV-halo transition system.

AI.tldr: First detection of radio pulsations from PSR J2238+5903 (a gamma-ray pulsar coincident with TeV source 1LHAASO J2238+5900) using FAST. The pulsar shows P=162.77 ms, DM=247.5 pc cm⁻³, and extremely faint flux density (~3 μJy). DM-based distance estimates (7.4±3.9 kpc) enable assessment of this system as a potential relic-PWN/TeV-halo transition object.
AI.motivation: To confirm the radio pulsar counterpart of the gamma-ray pulsar PSR J2238+5903, which is spatially coincident with the extended TeV source 1LHAASO J2238+5900, and to provide a pulsar-specific distance constraint via DM for studying the nature of the TeV emission (relic PWN vs. TeV halo).
AI.method: 3000 s FAST L-band observation; periodic signal search using both FFT-based and Fast Folding Algorithm (FFA) methods; flux density estimation via the radiometer equation; distance estimation using Galactic electron-density models applied to the measured DM.
AI.result: Detection of weak periodic radio signal at P=162.76568 ms, DM=247.5±3.0 pc cm⁻³, flux density S₁₂₅₀≈3 μJy (among faintest radio-detected Fermi pulsars). DM-inferred distance d_DM=7.4±3.9 kpc; at this distance the TeV source containment radius corresponds to ~132 pc diameter, and L_TeV≈7.1×10³⁴ erg s⁻¹ (~8% of pulsar spin-down power).
AI.conclusion: The radio DM provides the first pulsar-specific distance constraint, enabling assessment of whether 1LHAASO J2238+5900 represents a young relic-PWN/TeV-halo transition system.

title: The DESI View of the Faint Radio Source Population in LoTSS DR2
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The faint radio-source population includes galaxies dominated by both star formation (SF) and active galactic nuclei (AGN), which are two key processes shaping galaxy evolution. To investigate this population, we probabilistically classified 251,413 radio sources from the second data release of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS DR2) using spectroscopic data from the first release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1). Our classification method includes: (i) the identification of radio excess relative to SF, (ii) the Baldwin, Philips & Terlevich (BPT) diagram, (iii) a modified Mass Excitation (MEx) diagram, and (iv) the [OIII]5007 equivalent width. These are combined with Monte Carlo methods to estimate the probability that each source is a star-forming galaxy (SFG), a radio-quiet AGN (RQ AGN), or a low- or high-excitation radio galaxy (LERG or HERG), allowing various thresholds to be applied depending on science goals. Considering classifications above a 90 per cent probability threshold, we identify 68,820 SFGs, 32,288 RQ AGN, 35,210 LERGs and 3,085 HERGs, representing the largest radio sample to date with high-confidence spectroscopic classifications. Using this sample, we show with higher statistical power than previous studies that LERGs typically accrete below 1 per cent of the Eddington limit and HERGs above it. We also identify a small subset of high-accreting LERGs whose stacked spectra reveal prominent star-forming features, highlighting difficulties in interpreting their accretion properties. Our results demonstrate the power of large spectroscopic samples to characterise the radio-source population, providing a foundation for studies in the SKA era.

AI.tldr: Using DESI DR1 spectroscopy, we probabilistically classified 251,413 radio sources from LoTSS DR2 into SFGs, RQ AGN, LERGs, and HERGs. At 90% confidence, we identified 139,403 sources (the largest such radio sample to date), showing LERGs accrete below 1% Eddington and HERGs above it, with a subset of high-accreting LERGs showing star-forming features.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the faint radio-source population, which includes both star formation and AGN contributions, in order to better understand the roles these two processes play in galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Probabilistic classification of 251,413 LoTSS DR2 sources using DESI DR1 spectroscopy, combining: (i) radio excess relative to SF, (ii) BPT diagram, (iii) modified Mass Excitation diagram, and (iv) [OIII]5007 equivalent width, integrated with Monte Carlo methods to assign probabilities for SFG, RQ AGN, LERG, and HERG classes.
AI.result: At >90% probability threshold: 68,820 SFGs, 32,288 RQ AGN, 35,210 LERGs, 3,085 HERGs. LERGs accrete below 1% Eddington limit, HERGs above it. A small subset of high-accreting LERGs show prominent star-forming features in stacked spectra.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrated the power of large spectroscopic samples for characterizing the radio-source population, providing a robust foundation for future studies in the SKA era.

title: Active galactic nuclei are not responsible for systematics in the empirical properties of type Ia supernovae
comment: Published in RNAAS - This is an author compiled version. 3 Pages, 1 Figure
summary: Despite being key cosmological anchors, the empirical properties of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) remain subject to significant systematic uncertainties, the largest of which being their astrophysics and how this is linked to their environment. The relative importance of these uncertainties will grow as larger observational samples reduce statistical uncertainties. Here I explore if the presence of an active galactic nucleus (AGN) within a portion of SN Ia host galaxies could be one such systematic uncertainty. With the ZTF SNe Ia DR2 sample I find that, in the low redshift regime (z < 0.15), the presence of AGNs in some SN Ia hosts does not produce a significant systematic effect on their measured Hubble residuals.

AI.tldr: Type Ia supernova Hubble residuals are not significantly affected by the presence of AGNs in their host galaxies (z < 0.15, ZTF DR2 sample).
AI.motivation: SN Ia systematic uncertainties, especially those related to astrophysics and environment, remain large and will become more important as statistical errors shrink. The paper investigates whether AGN presence in host galaxies contributes to these systematics.
AI.method: Using the ZTF SNe Ia DR2 sample, the author compares Hubble residuals of SNe Ia hosted in galaxies with and without AGNs, focusing on the low-redshift regime (z < 0.15).
AI.result: The presence of AGNs in some SN Ia host galaxies does not produce a significant systematic effect on measured Hubble residuals at z < 0.15.
AI.conclusion: AGN activity in host galaxies is not a major source of systematic uncertainty for SN Ia cosmology in the low-redshift regime, at least for the ZTF DR2 sample.

title: On the detection of Population III galaxies: Emission Line Diagnostics for Hybrid Stellar Populations
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Identifying Population III (Pop III) stars, the first generation of metal-free stars in the early Universe, remains a central challenge in astrophysics. High-ionization emission lines, such as HeII are commonly used as tracers of Pop III signatures. However, realistic galaxies may host hybrid stellar populations, including both Pop III and metal-enriched Population II (Pop II) stars, complicating the interpretation of observed spectra. We aim to investigate how hybrid Pop III/Pop II stellar populations affect emission line diagnostics and assess the detectability of Pop III stars across different galactic environments and redshifts. We select galaxies with varying Pop III-to-total mass ratios from the IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations. Using self-consistent photoionisation models, we compute integrated spectra by adopting local physical conditions from the simulations to study the resulting emission line diagnostics. We find that emission line diagnostics are strongly dependent on the relative Pop III contribution. Current diagnostics can identify galaxies dominated totally by Pop III stars but fail for systems where Pop II stars contribute significantly, introducing degeneracies in interpreting observed spectra. Our results highlight the limitations of existing emission line diagnostics in hybrid systems and emphasize the need for additional methods that account for mixed stellar populations to reliably detect Pop III stars during and after the epoch of reionization.

AI.tldr: This study shows that current emission line diagnostics (like HeII) can detect galaxies purely composed of Pop III stars, but fail for realistic hybrid Pop III/Pop II systems due to degeneracies, highlighting the need for new methods that account for mixed stellar populations.
AI.motivation: Identifying Population III stars is a central challenge in astrophysics, and hybrid Pop III/Pop II stellar populations complicate the interpretation of observed spectra.
AI.method: Galaxies with varying Pop III-to-total mass ratios are selected from IllustrisTNG cosmological simulations; self-consistent photoionisation models compute integrated spectra using local physical conditions from the simulations to study emission line diagnostics.
AI.result: Emission line diagnostics strongly depend on the relative Pop III contribution; current diagnostics can identify Pop III-dominated galaxies but fail for systems with significant Pop II contribution due to degeneracies.
AI.conclusion: Existing emission line diagnostics are limited in hybrid systems, emphasizing the need for additional methods that account for mixed stellar populations to reliably detect Pop III stars during and after the epoch of reionization.

title: Hα clarifies picture of IIn supernova SN 2015da
summary: Observational data on type IIn supernova SN 2015da are revisited to clarify some ambiguous issues of this phenomenon. The H alpha--emitting site is found to switch around day 90 from the circumstellar matter to the unshocked ejecta. This picture makes it possible to recover the expansion velocity of late time ejecta and to locate the dust formation in the inner zone of unshocked ejecta.The bolometric light curve and expansion velocities combined with modelling the circumstellar interaction imply that the supernova exploded with an energy of $\gtrsim 4\times10^{51}$ erg inside the circumstellar envelope with the mass of $\approx 14$ Msun. The recovered density of the circumstellar matter is consistent with the Thomson optical depth inferred from H alpha modelling on day 46.The observed circumstellar envelope is produced by an average mass loss rate of 0.035 Msun/yr during 400 yr before the supernova explosion.

AI.tldr: Reanalysis of SN 2015da shows the Hα-emitting site switches from circumstellar matter to unshocked ejecta around day 90, revealing a supernova explosion energy ≥4×10⁵¹ erg within a ~14 M☉ circumstellar envelope, with an average mass loss rate of 0.035 M☉/yr over 400 yr prior to explosion.
AI.motivation: To clarify ambiguous issues in the observational data of type IIn supernova SN 2015da by revisiting the Hα emission site and circumstellar interaction.
AI.method: Reanalysis of observational data including Hα emission site tracking, bolometric light curve and expansion velocity modeling, and circumstellar interaction modeling.
AI.result: Hα-emitting site switches from circumstellar matter to unshocked ejecta around day 90; explosion energy ≥4×10⁵¹ erg; circumstellar envelope mass ~14 M☉; average mass loss rate 0.035 M☉/yr over 400 yr before explosion; dust formation occurs in inner unshocked ejecta; Thomson optical depth from Hα modeling on day 46 is consistent with recovered CSM density.
AI.conclusion: The reanalysis resolves ambiguities in SN 2015da, establishing a clear picture of the emission site transition, dust formation location, and constraining the progenitor's mass loss history and explosion energetics.

title: Enhancing Photometric Redshift Estimation for LSST with a Hybrid LSTM-Mixture Density Network
summary: Accurate photometric redshift (photo-$z$) estimation and robust uncertainty quantification are essential for the LSST to achieve its precision cosmology goals. Traditional machine learning algorithms are largely restricted to point estimates, struggling to characterize the multimodal nature of redshift PDFs and the degeneracies within the color-redshift space. To address this, we present and validate the LSTM-MDNz architecture, which integrates sequential feature extraction with flexible probability density modeling to enhance both prediction accuracy and uncertainty calibration across a broad redshift range, thereby meeting the stringent data quality requirements necessitated by next-generation cosmological analysis. The LSTM-MDNz framework treats multi-band photometry as wavelength-ordered sequences, utilizing LSTM networks to capture non-linear evolutionary correlations across the SED. A Mixture Density Network (MDN) is then employed to explicitly model posterior PDFs via Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). Performance is evaluated on the HSC GalaxiesML dataset (which serves as a small-scale proxy for next-generation surveys like LSST) and benchmarked against the BNN architecture established by Jones et al. (2024). The proposed model consistently outperforms the BNN baseline, achieving a $\sim 10\%$ improvement in point-estimation accuracy (specifically across RMSE, MAE, scatter, and $σ_{\text{NMAD}}$) and a $\sim 20\%$ reduction in the rates of both general and catastrophic outliers. A uniform probability integral transform (PIT) distribution confirms well-calibrated probabilistic outputs. Furthermore, the PDF-based confidence metric $z_{\text{conf}}$ enables high-purity catalog construction: excluding just approximately $4\%$ of extremely low-confidence ($z_{\text{conf}} < 0.05$) samples reduces the overall outlier rate by $\sim 48\%$.

AI.tldr: The LSTM-MDNz architecture integrates LSTM feature extraction with Mixture Density Networks to improve photometric redshift estimation and uncertainty quantification, achieving ~10% better point-estimation accuracy and ~20% fewer outliers compared to BNN baselines on the HSC GalaxiesML dataset, with well-calibrated PDFs enabling high-purity catalog construction.
AI.motivation: Accurate photo-z estimation and robust uncertainty quantification are critical for LSST precision cosmology, but traditional ML methods produce only point estimates and fail to capture multimodal redshift PDFs and color-redshift degeneracies.
AI.method: LSTM-MDNz treats multi-band photometry as wavelength-ordered sequences, using LSTM networks to capture non-linear SED correlations, then applies a Mixture Density Network (MDN) to model posterior PDFs via Gaussian mixture models (GMMs).
AI.result: Outperforms BNN baseline with ~10% improvement in point-estimation accuracy (RMSE, MAE, scatter, σ_NMAD) and ~20% reduction in outlier rates; uniform PIT distribution confirms calibration; excluding ~4% low-confidence (z_conf<0.05) samples reduces outlier rate by ~48%.
AI.conclusion: LSTM-MDNz provides accurate, well-calibrated photo-z PDFs suitable for next-generation cosmological surveys, with effective confidence-based filtering for high-purity catalog construction.

title: Tilted thin accretion disks in the full Kerr spacetime and their implications
comment: 25 pages, 17 figures, 2 tables, accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. D
summary: We derive a steady-state warped-disk equation in the full Kerr spacetime to study the tilt dynamics of a thin, viscous accretion disk around a spinning collapsed object. The formulation, based on Pringle's framework, remains valid for all values of the Kerr parameter $a$, thereby encompassing both Kerr black holes (BHs; $0 < a \le 1$) and Kerr naked singularities ($a > 1$). By incorporating the exact Keplerian and Lense-Thirring precession frequencies, we analytically obtain the radial tilt profiles of the disk without invoking slow-spin or weak-field approximations. Numerical solutions of the resulting equations, obtained under realistic boundary conditions, reveal significant deviations from slow-spin approximations, particularly in the inner disk where the relativistic effects dominate. In the diffusive regime, we find that for Kerr naked singularities the tilt profile exhibits distinct inner hump(s) near the radius where the specific angular momentum vanishes -- a feature absent for Kerr BHs. Consideration of a tilt in the inner disk could significantly influence the interpretations from observed X-ray spectral, timing, and polarization features, which are crucial to probe the strong gravity regime and to infer the spin of the central object. While such a distinct hump feature alone does not uniquely distinguish Kerr BHs from Kerr naked singularities, their interpretation in conjunction with constraints on the disk regime may provide a potential observational handle on the nature of the accreting collapsed object.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a steady-state warped-disk equation in full Kerr spacetime for thin viscous accretion disks, applicable to both Kerr black holes (a ≤ 1) and naked singularities (a > 1). Without slow-spin approximations, the analytic tilt profiles show significant deviations from weak-field limits. For Kerr naked singularities, a distinct inner tilt hump appears near the vanishing angular momentum radius, which could aid in distinguishing the nature of the central object when combined with disk regime constraints.
AI.motivation: To study tilt dynamics of thin viscous accretion disks around spinning collapsed objects (Kerr BHs and naked singularities) using full relativistic treatment, without relying on slow-spin or weak-field approximations, and to identify observational signatures that could distinguish between BHs and naked singularities.
AI.method: Derivation of a steady-state warped-disk equation in full Kerr spacetime using Pringle's framework, incorporating exact Keplerian and Lense-Thirring precession frequencies, followed by numerical solutions under realistic boundary conditions for both diffusive and likely wave-like regimes.
AI.result: Significant deviations from slow-spin approximations are found in the inner disk. For Kerr naked singularities (a > 1), the tilt profile shows distinct inner hump(s) near the radius where specific angular momentum vanishes, a feature absent for Kerr BHs (a ≤ 1).
AI.conclusion: The hump feature alone cannot uniquely distinguish Kerr BHs from naked singularities, but combined with disk regime constraints it may provide observational handles for probing strong gravity, potentially influencing interpretations of X-ray spectral, timing, and polarization data.

title: There is no single density: star-forming regions and galaxies hold more dense ionized gas than long assumed
comment: Submitted manuscript; comments welcome
summary: Ionized gas fills star-forming regions and galaxies, and nearly everything we know about its temperature, pressure, mass, and composition is inferred from its emission lines [1-3]. The electron density is needed for all of these, yet a longstanding puzzle has resisted explanation: different density-sensitive lines, applied to the same gas, return values that disagree by up to two orders of magnitude. This is usually attributed either to each line tracing a physically distinct ionization zone or to imperfect atomic data [4-7]. Here we show that the disagreement is neither a flaw in the atomic data nor an ionization-stratification effect, but something more fundamental. Each diagnostic is tuned to a particular density, and when a nebula contains gas across a wide range of densities, as real nebulae do, each line reports the part of that range it is most sensitive to. The diagnostics do not measure a representative average density; they respond to different parts of a broad density distribution. This resolves the discrepancy with a simple relation between the density each line returns and the density it is most sensitive to, a relation that holds from individual H II regions to whole galaxies, near and far, and reveals that ionized nebulae contain far more dense gas than any one diagnostic implies. A nebula has no single electron density to measure, but a broad density distribution, and the masses, pressures, abundances and energetics built on the single-density assumption must be reconsidered, from nearby star-forming regions to galaxies across cosmic time.

AI.tldr: Disagreements among electron density diagnostics in ionized nebulae are not due to atomic data flaws or ionization stratification, but because each diagnostic is sensitive to a different part of the broad density distribution present in real nebulae, meaning there is no single representative electron density.
AI.motivation: A long-standing puzzle exists where different density-sensitive emission lines applied to the same ionized gas return electron density values that disagree by up to two orders of magnitude, previously attributed to distinct ionization zones or imperfect atomic data.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate that each density diagnostic is tuned to a particular density; in real nebulae with a wide range of densities, each line reports the part of that range it is most sensitive to, rather than a representative average. A simple relation between the returned density and the diagnostic's sensitivity peak resolves the discrepancy.
AI.result: The relation holds from individual H II regions to entire galaxies, both nearby and distant, and reveals that ionized nebulae contain far more dense gas than any single diagnostic implies.
AI.conclusion: Ionized nebulae possess a broad density distribution rather than a single electron density. Measurements of masses, pressures, abundances, and energetics built on the single-density assumption must be reconsidered across all scales.

title: SACRA-K: A Performance-Portable Numerical Relativity Code with Kokkos
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures
summary: We present SACRA-K (SimulAtor for Compact objects in Relativistic Astrophysics with Kokkos), a performance-portable numerical relativity code ported from the Fortran code SACRA-MPI to C++ with the Kokkos library. SACRA-K retains the physics and numerical methods of SACRA-MPI, namely a Baumgarte-Shapiro-Shibata-Nakamura (BSSN) spacetime evolution with Z4c constraint propagation and a box-in-box Berger-Oliger adaptive mesh refinement, together with the high resolution shock capturing scheme for the general relativistic hydrodynamics from NANASI, while gaining cross vendor portability. We validate the port against SACRA-MPI across binary black hole, black hole neutron star, and binary neutron star configurations. Across these tests, the waveform discrepancies are well below both the scatter among independent numerical relativity codes and the resolution dependent variation within a given code, and remain at or below the distinguishability threshold of current gravitational-wave detectors; the $π$ symmetry is preserved exactly at the bitwise level; and the gravitational wave phase of the binary neutron star merger exhibits second order convergence. In the smallest test configuration, SACRA-K runs about an order of magnitude faster on the NVIDIA A100 GPU cluster or the AMD MI300A APU cluster than the Fortran SACRA-MPI on the CPU cluster, and we measure its scaling up to 256 accelerator devices.

AI.tldr: SACRA-K is a performance-portable numerical relativity code ported from Fortran SACRA-MPI to C++ using Kokkos, validated across binary black hole, BH-NS, and binary neutron star configurations, showing waveform discrepancies below detection thresholds, exact π symmetry, and ~10x speedup on NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI300A accelerators.
AI.motivation: To create a performance-portable numerical relativity code that retains the physics and numerics of SACRA-MPI while gaining cross-vendor portability (NVIDIA, AMD) and leveraging accelerator hardware.
AI.method: Ported SACRA-MPI from Fortran to C++ using the Kokkos library, implementing BSSN spacetime evolution with Z4c constraint propagation, box-in-box Berger-Oliger adaptive mesh refinement, and high-resolution shock capturing for GRHD.
AI.result: Waveform discrepancies are well below scatter among independent NR codes and resolution-dependent variation, at or below the distinguishability threshold of current GW detectors; π symmetry preserved at bitwise level; BNS merger GW phase exhibits second-order convergence; ~10x speedup on A100 and MI300A vs. Fortran on CPU; scaling up to 256 accelerators.
AI.conclusion: SACRA-K successfully achieves performance portability across CPU and GPU architectures while maintaining the accuracy and reliability of SACRA-MPI, enabling efficient numerical relativity simulations on diverse hardware.

title: CARPP: Parametric Radiative-Transfer Fitting of Molecular Cores from Dust Continuum Data
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: The density profiles of dense molecular cores are important indicators of their physical and evolutionary states. Multi-wavelength dust continuum data offers excellent constraints on the density profile of cores. Here we introduce CARPP (Core Analysis via Radiative Transfer and Profile Parameters), a publicly available fitting package that generates optimized core density and temperature profiles based on parameterized radiative transfer calculations. CARPP assumes spherical symmetry and adopts physically motivated parametric forms for the density and temperature profiles, and uses dust continuum data for fitting. Tests on synthetic data show that CARPP achieves high accuracy, namely averaged relative errors of CARPP's seven parameters being $<20\%$, when the data quality satisfies $\frac{\rm RMS \,\, noise}{[\rm peak \,\, flux]} < 0.025\times \frac{[r_0]}{\rm resolution} +0.05$, where $r_0$ is the core's characteristic radius. We select the low-mass core TMC-1C and the high-mass core Ori2-2 to demonstrate CARPP's performance on real data. It classifies TMC-1C as a Bonnor-Ebert sphere in near-hydrostatic equilibrium, while Ori2-2 exhibits a power-law-dominated profile indicative of a collapsing envelope. This capability establishes CARPP as a powerful and versatile tool to classify the dynamical states of individual cores. It offers an optimal balance between physical fidelity and computational efficiency, serving as a practical, standardized alternative to both over-simplified SED analyses and complex, time-intensive 3D radiative-transfer modeling.

AI.tldr: CARPP is a publicly available fitting package that generates optimized density and temperature profiles of dense molecular cores from multi-wavelength dust continuum data, achieving high accuracy and classifying core dynamical states (e.g., hydrostatic equilibrium vs. collapsing envelope).
AI.motivation: Density profiles of dense molecular cores are key indicators of their physical and evolutionary states, and multi-wavelength dust continuum data can provide strong constraints, but a practical, standardized tool for efficient yet physically faithful inference was lacking.
AI.method: CARPP assumes spherical symmetry, adopts physically motivated parametric forms for density and temperature profiles, and performs parameterized radiative transfer calculations fitted to dust continuum data.
AI.result: On synthetic data, CARPP achieves average relative errors <20% for its seven parameters when data quality meets a derived criterion. On real data, it classifies TMC-1C as a Bonnor-Ebert sphere (near-hydrostatic equilibrium) and Ori2-2 as a power-law-dominated collapsing envelope.
AI.conclusion: CARPP is a powerful, versatile tool for classifying the dynamical states of individual cores, offering an optimal balance between physical fidelity and computational efficiency as a standardized alternative to both simple SED analyses and expensive 3D radiative-transfer modeling.
